1. Model consistently overestimates prices in the early part of the 30-day forecast, especially after recent spikes — reduce initial forecast values by 1–3% to align with observed mean reversion.

2. Model underestimates prices in the final 5–10 days of the forecast — increase end-of-horizon values by 1–2% to reflect downward momentum or policy-induced corrections.

3. After a price spike (e.g., >88), model tends to overshoot and then overcorrect — dampen forecast peaks by 2–5% and smooth transitions to avoid excessive volatility.

4. Model exhibits persistent bias toward lower prices in the first 10 days — adjust downward by 0.5–1.5% for early forecast periods if recent history shows downward trend.

5. Model fails to capture mean reversion in the middle of the forecast — if 15-day average of history is >85, reduce forecast by 1–2% for next 5 days to reflect expected pullback.

6. Model often ignores short-term policy or emission cap adjustments — if historical data shows sudden policy change (e.g., cap tightening), reduce forecast by 2–4% for next 3–5 days.
